fixes.explanation: Right on the money, baker. The text says Aquila and Priscilla were tentmakers by trade, just as Paul was. Same trade, so staying and working with them made sense. When I find somebody else who loves a good rolling pin, I'm there all day too.
Yes, baker. The text says Paul was trying to persuade Jews and Greeks alike, every Sabbath. So the synagogue crowd wasn't only Jews. Paul was talking to both groups.
That's the one, baker. Paul was testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ. Once Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, he devoted himself fully to the word.

I see where that came from, friend, but it's not what the text says. Paul testified to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ (Acts 18:5). That happened after Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia. The Christ is the title he put in front of them.

Good guess, but there's no angel in this verse, baker. After Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul devoted himself fully to the word. He testified to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ. It's one short line, and it's the center of the verse.

True, baker. Crispus, the synagogue leader, and his whole household believed in the Lord. The man in charge of the synagogue, and his whole household with him! Paul had left that synagogue after being opposed and insulted (Acts 18:6), and still its leader believed. I'd have needed to sit down.

Yes, baker. Many of the Corinthians who heard the message believed and were baptized. Hearing, believing, baptism: the verse lays it out in that order. That's a lot of people packed into one sentence.

That's not the word here, baker. The text says many of the Corinthians who heard the message believed and were baptized (Acts 18:8). Nothing in that verse scatters anybody. Those who heard believed, and those who believed were baptized.

That's right, baker. The Lord said, “For I am with you and no one will lay a hand on you, because I have many people in this city.” Two promises in one line: He is with Paul, and no one will lay a hand on him. The reason He gives is that He has many people in this city.

That's a nice thought, baker, but the Lord doesn't say it. He told Paul, “For I am with you and no one will lay a hand on you, because I have many people in this city.” The reason He gives for no one laying a hand on Paul is that He has many people in this city.

You got it, baker. Paul stayed for a year and a half, teaching the word of God among the Corinthians. That's a long stretch in one place. I've spent longer than that stuck in the back of a junk drawer, so I know a long stay.
That's too short, friend. The text says Paul stayed for a year and a half, teaching the word of God among the Corinthians. Three months is a small slice of that. He settled in for the long haul.
It might seem that way, baker, but the text doesn't show it. Just as Paul was about to speak, Gallio, the proconsul, told the Jews his answer. The text gives no defense from Paul in that scene.

That's right, baker. Just as Paul was about to speak, Gallio, the proconsul, spoke to the Jews instead. The text gives no defense from Paul in that scene. I think that was a strange moment, being ready to talk and then not needed.

Nothing about owning the synagogue shows up in what Gallio says, friend. He called it “…a dispute about words and names and your own law…” That's a quarrel over words, names and law, not over who holds the keys.
Land never comes up, baker. Gallio told the Jews, “But since it is a dispute about words and names and your own law, settle it yourselves.” No fences, no property lines, just words, names and law.
True, baker. Gallio said, “…settle it yourselves.” Then he added, “I refuse to be a judge of such things.” He was the proconsul sitting at the judgment seat, and he still handed it back.
